ABSTRACT

RAINFALL-DRIVEN VARIABILITY OF PHYSICOCHEMICAL WATER QUALITY PARAMETERS IN THE MEGHNA RIVER, BANGLADESH: A PRELIMINARY MONTHLY ASSESSMENT USING CORRELATION, REGRESSION, AND PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author: Abu Bakor Siddique Patwary.

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.02.2026.138.143

Rainfall governs much of the month-to-month variability seen in the physicochemical condition of tropical rivers, acting through two competing mechanisms: dilution of dissolved constituents during high flow, and wash-off of organic and inorganic material from the surrounding catchment. This study examines how monthly rainfall relates to five water-quality parameters — pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), total dissolved solids (TDS), and chemical oxygen demand (COD) — at the Meghna Ghat monitoring station on the Meghna River, Bangladesh, during 2023. Water-quality records were obtained from the Bangladesh Department of Environment (DoE), and monthly rainfall totals were derived from NASA’s Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) database. Because DoE monitoring at this station was incomplete during 2023, a full set of water-quality observations was available for only six months (n = 6). Pearson correlation showed a very strong positive association between rainfall and COD (r = 0.99, p < 0.001), together with moderate negative associations between rainfall and both BOD (r = −0.71) and TDS (r = −0.62) — consistent with a combined dilution/wash-off response. Rainfall was not significantly related to a composite Water Quality Index (WQI) built from the five parameters (r = −0.46, p = 0.36). A complementary principal component analysis (PCA) on the standardized six-month dataset accounted for 85.3% of total variance, with the leading component loading heavily on rainfall, COD, BOD, and TDS, reinforcing the correlation findings. Given the very small sample size, these results should be read as a preliminary, hypothesis-generating baseline rather than a definitive account of rainfall–water-quality dynamics on the Meghna.
